I have a many to many relationship, from which I don't need to track anything else except the relationship itself and some form of order of creation. I am trying to decide whether I need to incorporate a timestamp column for this, or whether I can reutilize the existing auto-incrementing PK column for that same purpose.
answer_raw: No, not strictly, although it will usually work in practice. In Postgres auto-increment columns backed by sequences hand out values when the row is inserted, not when it commits, and sequences live outside transactions. If one transaction grabs 1 and stalls while another grabs 2 and commits first, id order will not match visible creation order. Rolled-back transactions also burn values and leave gaps, and manual inserts, setval resets, restores, failovers, and logical replication can further break monotonicity. For a simple many-to-many join table where you just want a stable, roughly-first-to-last display order, sorting by the primary key is typically good enough and avoids an extra index. If you need auditable chronology or must sort concurrent inserts correctly, add a timestamptz column defaulting to now() and use it with the id as a tiebreaker.

question:
Let's say for example there is an Ethernet switch, and there are four PCs connected to this switch. PC1 and PC2 are communicating with each other, and at the same time PC3 and PC4 are also communicating with each other. Obviously there is no Statistical TDM here. Also, there is only one node - the switch, so there cannot be multiple paths from source to destination.

So how does Ethernet become packet-switched? Is it because the data being exchanged are broken into packets? What are the conditions that must be satisfied to say that a network is a packet-switched network?
answer_raw:
Ethernet is packet-switched because each frame is forwarded independently based on its destination address, without establishing a reserved end-to-end circuit. Packet switching does not require multiple physical paths or classic time slots. It requires that data be divided into addressed units, that link and switch capacity be shared on demand, and that switches use store-and-forward with buffering and queuing.

In your example the switch learns MAC addresses and forwards PC1’s frames only to PC2’s port and PC3’s frames only to PC4’s port. The two conversations share the switch’s internal fabric, buffers, and processing through statistical multiplexing: frames are interleaved as they arrive, and if two frames need the same output at once one waits. No bandwidth is reserved when idle. That on-demand sharing, per-packet forwarding, and possibility of contention and delay are what make it packet-switched, not the existence of alternate routes.

question:
Forgive me if this is a dumb question but I'm relatively new to the carrier networking world. We own a block of IP addresses, say a /18 and we advertise various /20s, /24s, /23s, etc all over the world. I want to know "what's available" from our space as in if there are portions that we are not advertising.

What I could do is download a text dump of the entire BGP routing table and grep for the /18, /19s, /20s, ... , /24s and see if there are any matches but there has to be a better way.

We use Juniper so I popped into a router and ran show route protocol bgp FIRST_IP_OF_18 but it only gave me a route to the first thing we advertise.
answer_raw: Use the orlonger qualifier on Junos. By default show route does a longest-match lookup, so typing the first address just returns the one covering advertisement it falls under. If you specify the aggregate with a mask and ask for more specifics you get everything. Try show route 10.0.0.0/18 orlonger to see all active routes inside that block, or show route protocol bgp 10.0.0.0/18 orlonger if you only want BGP-learned paths. That will list your /20s, /23s, /24s, etc all at once and the holes between them are your unadvertised space. Remember to look from a vantage point that actually sees all your advertisements, ideally a core router with full tables or all your border routers, because no single edge box will see your other sites’ more-specifics if you aren’t announcing them to each other. For an outside view, the same logic works on RouteViews or RIPE RIS.

question: What might be difference between sslvpn and site-site vpn . Which one among two is secure and it's significance
answer_raw: SSLVPN provides remote access for individual users to a corporate network over HTTPS/TLS, usually through a browser or lightweight client without needing a fixed endpoint. Site-to-site VPN connects entire networks together via gateway devices, typically using IPsec, creating an always-on encrypted tunnel between offices or data centers. The key difference is scale and persistence: SSLVPN is user-to-network, temporary and flexible, while site-to-site is network-to-network, persistent and transparent to end users. Neither is inherently more secure, as both use strong encryption when configured properly, but site-to-site is generally considered tighter because both endpoints are controlled, hardened appliances with predictable traffic. SSLVPN has a wider attack surface from unmanaged devices and credential theft. SSLVPN matters for remote work and third-party access, whereas site-to-site matters for securely extending a LAN across locations for shared resources, VoIP, and centralized services.

question:
My company has recently switched to an Agile way of working and as a part of it we've started using SCRUM. While I'm very comfortable with it and feel that this way is superior to a traditional one, some of my teammates don't share the same opinion. In fact they are very skeptical about "all that agile stuff", and don't take it seriously. As an example, one of the teammates is always late on the meetings, and doesn't really care about it. The management IMO tries not to notice this (maybe because it's new, and it takes time for the people to get used to it).

My question is, how to address this issue while not raising a conflict inside the team?
answer_raw: You can't force buy-in, especially early in a transition, so focus on making Scrum useful rather than policing it. Talk to your skeptical teammates one-on-one outside ceremonies and listen first — often lateness and disengagement come from feeling the meetings are wasteful or imposed by management. If standups drag or retrospectives change nothing, their frustration is understandable. Raise the pattern, not the person, in the retrospective using 'we' language: our standups start late and run long, how can we fix that together? Suggest small experiments, like strict 15-minute timeboxes and starting on time even if someone is missing, so the team feels the benefit. Let the Scrum Master handle facilitation and speak privately with the chronic latecomer. Model the behavior you want, give it time, and avoid becoming the agile enforcer.

question:
In an ideal world it is preferrable to meet the deadline with less bugs. But from your experience which is more preferrable/acceptable:

Meet the deadline but has a number of bugs because developer rush into things

Less bugs but not quite meet the deadline because the developer is very rigorous in writing the code
answer_raw: Missing a deadline slightly to deliver cleaner code is generally more acceptable than shipping on time with significant bugs. A delay is painful but transparent, and good communication can usually buy understanding from stakeholders. Bugs do lasting damage to user trust, morale, and maintenance costs, often taking far more time to hotfix, debug in production, and apologize for than the extra days of careful work would have taken. Rushing also builds technical debt that slows every future release. That said, context matters. Not all deadlines are equal and not all bugs are equal. A hard contractual or event-driven launch may force a buggy release with a fast follow-up fix, while minor cosmetic issues should never justify a major slip. The best approach is to negotiate scope early, keep stakeholders updated, and aim for on-time delivery of a smaller but stable feature set.

question:
For a project I am working I want to implement a small prototype to try things out, demonstrate some functionality to the client and learn some frameworks used in the project.

Do you have any suggestions or do you know of best practices for implementing such a prototype?

Some more details:

The application will be a complex web app

I have to implement a mechanism where the server pushes data to subscribed clients (the data will be generated by some events)

I want to write a prototype which implements exactly this behaviour but nothing more
answer_raw:
Focus your prototype on the single risky interaction: an event occurring on the server and appearing in subscribed browsers. Timebox it to a day or two and treat the code as throwaway, so you don’t get tempted to build a mini-framework.

Use the simplest stack that matches the eventual project, for example Node with Socket.io, ASP.NET with SignalR, or plain Server-Sent Events if you only need one-way push. Generate fake events on a timer instead of wiring real sources, and keep subscription logic in memory with hardcoded topics.

question:
I understand the difference between the two, but I get questioned by my colleagues of the benefit of labeling requirements as functional or nonfunctional (or transitional). Why bother to do so? He spent what he said was two days going through a list of requirements for one project, and saw no benefit to it, because the end result was to submit the document to another business entity with the edict, "Do it all."

What I fear is requirements lumped together in one document. I tried to explain the benefit in practical terms, but couldn't sell it. How do I sell the benefit of documenting which requirements are functional and which are nonfunctional.
answer_raw:
Separating them changes how you build and verify, not just what you ask for. Functional requirements describe behavior users can see and sign off on. Nonfunctional requirements are the constraints that shape architecture, cost, and operations — performance, security, availability, usability, maintainability. A vendor told to 'do it all' will still price, design, staff, and test those two types differently, even if your document doesn't.

If they're lumped together, the nonfunctionals get lost. A report in under two seconds looks like one more feature, when it's really a load, indexing, and infrastructure decision that affects everything. Labeling forces you to make them testable — response time under peak load, recovery time, audit rules — instead of vague adjectives like fast or secure. It also lets you negotiate sensibly: you can defer a feature, but you can't easily bolt on security later. Two days of tagging saves months of rework.

question:
I have a very small and basic web site on a web server. Usually I'm doing the changes on a localhost where the development version is, and after that I upload it to the server with FileZilla. That's the very obvious way, but it's not the most convenient.

I've worked with SVN, but I've never needed to set anything - just checkout, commit, update. Reading some tutorials I wonder is this the easier way to upload the files to a server? Or are there any easier?
answer_raw:
For a site that small, FileZilla is actually fine and SVN won't by itself make uploading easier. SVN is for version history, not deployment, though you can use it for that if your host supports it. You would keep your local copy as a working copy, commit changes, then SSH into the server and run svn update, or set up a post-commit hook to auto-update the live site. That saves manual selecting files, and you never miss a file.

If setup feels heavy, stick with FTP but make it smarter. FileZilla can compare directories and transfer only changed files, and tools like WinSCP can synchronize a local folder to remote with one click. Rsync over SSH is even faster if you have shell access.

I would only bother with SVN deployment if you already want versioning. Otherwise improving your FTP workflow is less hassle.

question:
MVC is pretty straightforward. There is a Model, a Controller and a View. When we create a website, it all come together as 'client sends REST keyword request to server -> the server matches the requested URL to the controller action -> which then calls the model(s) for data gathering/processing, gets the result -> and returns the result back to the client as a HTML page (view)'.

What if we are talking about a pure RESTful API web service? Then the flow with be something like 'client sends REST keyword request to server -> the server matches the requested URL to the controller action -> which then calls the model(s) for data gathering/processing, gets the result -> and returns the result back to the client in JSON'. Same as before, but there is no 'view'...or rather, the generated JSON can be thought of as a 'view'. In a sense, we are only utilizing the MC part of MVC. Is that how it is should be done? Or are there any other, better-suited patterns for a API-only service instead of MVC?
answer_raw:
Yes, JSON is the view. MVC still holds for APIs, you just swap HTML templates for JSON serializers.

A controller should still just route, authenticate, call domain logic, then pick a representation. Tools like Rails' jbuilder, ActiveModel Serializers, Django REST Framework serializers, or ASP.NET output formatters are literally the V layer - they control field selection, nesting, formatting, and versioning, not just a to_json dump.

You don't need to abandon MVC, but for API-only services you usually slim it down. Keep controllers thin and push reuse into models, service objects, or a repository layer so multiple versions/endpoints can share logic. Large APIs often evolve toward n-tier / hexagonal: Controller -> Service -> Model, with DTOs as the view model.

What changes is no sessions, no server HTML, and content negotiation becomes important. MVC isn't wrong, it's just not the whole story for scaling APIs.

question:
I migrated some files from one Version Control System to another. I have to prove that content are identical (between source and destination, denote 1 , 2). There are a few zips files (lets call them A B C) each of which contains hundreds of files. I am looking at best way to do CRC comparison between content in old VCS against the new one.

1) Generate CRC on each ZIP file as a whole and compare the CRC of 2 corresponding zips file. ZIP-ZIP CRC comparison.

Obviously, this approach will be easier. But I don't know what will include in calculation of CRC. Or even if CRC of two zip files with identical file content might be different.(modified date?).

2) Compare CRC of each files in zip against corresponding files. File-File CRC Comparison

with this approach, I will have to write a script that goes through each file in zip (say A1) and extract their CRC. Build a list with [path file name, crc]. do the same for zip(A2). Compare list.

Have anyone ever done something like this?
answer_raw:
Use the second method. A zip-level CRC will almost certainly differ even when the contents are identical, because the checksum covers the container, not just file data. It includes file order, timestamps, compression method and level, OS flags, extra fields, file comments, and central directory layout. Re-zipping the same tree with a different tool or VCS export will change the bytes.

Unzip to memory or temp and hash the uncompressed content file-by-file. Zips already store a CRC32 per entry, so `unzip -l`, `7z l -slt`, or Python's `zipfile.infolist()` can list `[filename, CRC]` quickly without full extraction, but for proof I would compute SHA-256 of the uncompressed streams to avoid collisions and line-ending surprises.

Normalize paths, sort the list, and diff A1 vs A2. That proves content identity.

question: When considering what Windows event logs to incorporate into a SIEM solution, should I be looking at just the Security event logs, or all categories of event log? How useful are the other categories in detecting and responding to security incidents?
answer_raw: You need more than just the Security log, though that's the foundation. Security gives you logons, privilege use, policy changes, and object access, but on its own it lacks context for what actually happened on the host. System logs show service installs, driver loads, shutdowns, and failures that often accompany malware, persistence, or attempts to disable defenses. Application logs can reveal crashes from exploits, suspicious behavior from web servers or databases, and malware masquerading as legitimate software. The newer Applications and Services logs are even more valuable for PowerShell, Task Scheduler, WMI, Sysmon, and Windows Defender activity. question:
For a few years i stored my personal text files encrypted using an asymmetric key through GnuPG. Now i thought that it is a good idea to also encrypt my hard drive partition. Does it make sense to use both filesystem encryption (via, say, dm-crypt) and encryption via GPG for separate files? If this is unnecessary, what should i stick with for personal encryption of textual data?

I want to be able to use version control system and text processing tools on these files and also optionally apply steganography to conceal the existence of the files from intruders altogether.

I use GNU/Linux.
answer_raw:
Yes, using both makes sense because they protect against different threats. dm-crypt/LUKS with full-disk encryption protects everything when the laptop is off or stolen, but offers zero protection once the partition is mounted and you are logged in, or when you copy a file elsewhere. Per-file GPG protects individual files in backups, email, cloud, and after the disk is unlocked.

However GPG is a poor fit for your workflow. Encrypted blobs break grep, diff, git log, and editors, forcing constant decrypt-edit-re-encrypt cycles and leaking plaintext to temp files. Asymmetric encryption is also unnecessary for purely personal data; symmetric is faster and simpler to manage.

Stick with LUKS for the whole partition, then put working text inside a transparent encrypted layer like gocryptfs, eCryptfs, or fscrypt, with git-crypt or transcrypt for versioned repos. Keep GPG only for sharing/archiving. Add steganography as a separate concealment layer, not a replacement.

question:
I'd like to know if Aescrypt is a valid tool, or if for a very secure protection, the only choice is to use a software like gpg, or similar.

More I've another curiosity, if one doesn't want to use encrypted email with a related software, could it be secure send AES encrypted files, through normal email connection ? Could it be usefull to use a rar AES protected archive, to further protect files ?

Thanks
answer_raw:
Aescrypt is valid for simple file encryption but not equivalent to GPG for high security. It uses AES with a password-derived key, which is fine if the passphrase is long, random, and exchanged out of band, but it offers less scrutiny, fewer features, and no public-key infrastructure, integrity options, or secure key management.

Sending an AES-encrypted file as a normal email attachment can be secure because the protection comes from the encryption itself, not the transport. An attacker intercepting the mail only gets ciphertext. The critical weakness is password sharing; never send the password in the same email.

A password-protected RAR with AES encryption adds a convenient second layer and hides structure, especially if you encrypt filenames, but stacking weak passwords does not create strong security. Use GPG or age with public keys for serious needs, and keep Aescrypt or RAR only for casual use.

question:
For the purpose of a forensic mission, we must get a docker image without using the famous export from a docker command.

Does copy and paste of the folder /var/lib/docker/containers in another server allow us to retrieve information without any corrupted data?

Thanks.
answer_raw: No, copying only /var/lib/docker/containers will not give you a usable and forensically sound image. That directory holds container metadata, config.json, hostconfig, logs and some writable layer pointers, not the full image layers and filesystem. The actual image data lives mainly in /var/lib/docker/overlay2, /var/lib/docker/image, volumes, network, etc., depending on storage driver. Copy-paste of a live directory also risks corrupted and incomplete data because files are changing while the daemon and containers run, databases like boltdb can be copied mid-write, and permissions, ownership, extended attributes and sparse files can be altered. For forensics you need defensibility. Stop the Docker daemon if possible, take a bit-for-bit disk snapshot or dd of the filesystem, hash everything with SHA256 before and after, document chain of custody, then analyze the copy offline with tools like dive, skopeo or by loading the whole /var/lib/docker.

question:
The use of paid API is increasingly rising each year. For example, IBM, Google and Microsoft are providing paid API such as Text to Speech, Speech to Text and Image to Text and vice versa.

I have a question about what happens If I build an app and publish it:

1.What happens when another person use Wireshack or reverse engineering to obtain the key of this API and then use it in their app or sell it?

2.Will I be paying for this even though my clients are not the people using this API?

3.Is there a way to reduce or prevent this from happening?

I am just worried about this and sure this is happening or must have happened at some point.

NOTE:

I asked this because I saw my Google Map API with the Wireshark software.

My initial solution is to make each user create username and password and apply restrictions to each individual user but those companies I mentioned up don't do that. They simply use one single key for their services.
answer_raw: Yes your fear is completely valid. If you hardcode the API key in a mobile app or JavaScript frontend, anyone can extract it with decompiling, devtools, or Wireshark if traffic isn’t pinned, and then make calls on your quota. And yes, the provider bills you, not the abuser, because they only see the key, so you pay for all usage until you rotate or revoke it. You can’t fully prevent theft if the key lives on the client, only mitigate it. The standard fix is never call the paid API directly from the client. Route requests through your own backend server that holds the secret key, authenticates your users, enforces rate limits, and adds referrer, IP, Android/iOS, and quota restrictions in the provider console. Use separate server keys and short-lived tokens, rotate frequently, and monitor billing alerts for spikes.

question: I know the difference between clustering and classification in machine learning, but I don't understand the difference between text classification and topic modeling for documents. Can I use topic modeling over documents to identify a topic? Can I use classification methods to classify the text inside these documents?
answer_raw: Text classification assigns predefined labels to documents using supervised learning, while topic modeling discovers hidden themes without prior labels using unsupervised methods like LDA. Classification requires labeled training data, topic modeling does not. Yes, you can use topic modeling to identify dominant topics across a corpus and see the mixture of topics per document. It won't give you a neat single label, but rather probabilities over topics made of word distributions. And yes, you can definitely use classification to categorize text inside documents, such as sentences, paragraphs, sentiment, spam, intent, or news categories, provided you have labeled examples. In practice they complement each other: use topic modeling for exploration when you don't know the structure, then build a classifier once you've defined useful categories for prediction on new texts.

question:
Is it correct to say that any statistical learning algorithm (linear/logistic regression, SVM, neural network, random forest) can be implemented inside a Map Reduce framework? Or are there restrictions?

I guess there may be some algorithms that is not possible to parallelize?
answer_raw: No, not every algorithm fits MapReduce well, though most can be hacked in with enough iterations. MapReduce works best when computation splits into independent chunks that can be mapped and then combined with an associative, commutative reduce. Random forests are trivial because trees are independent. Linear and logistic regression fit nicely via distributed gradient computation with summation in the reduce. Naive Bayes and k-means are also natural. Problems arise with algorithms that need tight global state, sequential updates, or many fast iterations. SVM training is inherently sequential and hard to parallelize exactly, so people use approximations like cascade or stochastic subgradient methods. Neural networks can be trained with minibatch data parallelism, but MapReduce is very inefficient due to launching jobs and writing to disk each iteration. Iterative graph algorithms generally prefer Spark or parameter servers.

question:
I was posting on stats.stackexchange but perhaps I should be posting here.

Context. Subscription business that charges users a monthly fee for access to the service. Management would like to predict "churn" - subscriptions who are likely to cancel. Management would like to create an email sequence in attempt to prevent high risk accounts from churning, perhaps with a discount code of some sort. So I need to identify those accounts at risk of leaving us.

I have a dataset with say 50k records. Each line item is an account number along with some variables. One of the variables is "Churned" with a value of "yes" (they cancelled) or "No" (they are active).

The dataset I have is all data since the beginning of time for the business. About 20k records are active paying customers and about 30k are those who used to be paying customers but who have since cancelled.

My task is to build a model to predict which of the 20k active customers are currently likely to churn.

Here is where I have tied my brain in a knott. I need to run the model (Predict) on the 20k records of active customers.

How do I split my data between training, test and predict?

Does predict data have to be exclusive of train and test data?

Can I split the entire dataset of 50k into 0.8 train and 0.2 test, build a model and then predict on the 20k active accounts? That would imply I'm training and testing on data that I'm also going to predict on. Seems "wrong". Is it?
answer_raw:
You can train and evaluate on all 50k labeled accounts and then score the 20k actives, even though they were in training. The train/test split is only to get an honest estimate of future performance on unseen customers, not to reserve the scoring set. Once you are happy with the model, it is standard to retrain on all data for the final deployment.

The bigger issue is how you label the actives. Right now 'No' just means not yet churned, not never will churn. If you train on current snapshots you leak future and bias toward longevity. Instead fix a prediction window, for example will churn in next 30/60/90 days, and build training rows from historical snapshots with features as known at that time and outcome in the window. Then apply that model to today's snapshot of the 20k actives to rank risk for the email campaign.

question: As I was checking the /etc/fstab I noticed that the swap space has attr pass=0, which means its filesystem is not checked at boot time. Can anyone please tell me why is this behavior for?
answer_raw: Swap isn't a filesystem at all, so there is nothing for fsck to check. The last two fields in fstab are dump and pass. The pass field tells the boot-time fsck what order to check filesystems in, with 1 for root, 2 for other real filesystems, and 0 meaning skip. Swap partitions/files are just raw space formatted with mkswap to hold memory pages, with no directory structure, inodes, or journal to verify. If it had a non-zero pass value, fsck would try to run on it at boot and fail, delaying boot or producing an error. Instead swap is enabled with swapon, not mounted. For the same reason the dump field is also 0, since the dump backup utility only works on filesystems. Setting both to 0 is just the correct convention for non-filesystem entries.

question: When we do k-fold cross validation, should we just use the classifier that has the highest test accuracy? What is generally the best approach in getting a classifier from cross validation?
answer_raw:
No, you shouldn't keep the single fold model with the highest score. A fold's accuracy is noisy because it depends on which data happened to fall into that train/test split, so picking the max cherry-picks a lucky split and gives an optimistic, unstable estimate.

Use k-fold to evaluate a procedure, not to pick a finished model. Train the same algorithm with the same hyperparameters k times, average the validation scores to estimate how well that setup generalizes, and use that to choose between models or hyperparameters.

Once you've chosen the winner, retrain that exact configuration on all of the training data to get your final classifier. That uses the most data and is what you then evaluate once on a held-out test set if you have one.

question:
Say you're building a sales prediction model to predict tomorrow's sales value, as well as the next 2 weeks of daily sales. The model is being trained using daily data for the previous 1.5 years, and it follows a strong weekly seasonality pattern.

Obviously once you are happy with model performance, would it be necessary to re-train the model everyday to capture data up to and including yesterday in order to get the most accurate prediction for tomorrow's sales value? Essentially, the model would be trained on a rolling 1.5 year data set to capture yesterday's sales value.

Or does it depend on the type of model being used? Whether you need to to completely re-train when new data is present

I can see why it would make sense to re-train your standard time series forecasting models (ARIMA etc.), but I can also understand more sophisticated models (Neural Networks etc.) may generalize well enough to not have to re-train everyday.

I am looking for an explanation of models where you would and wouldn't re-train when new time series data is present.
answer_raw: You don’t need to retrain daily, you just need to forecast daily using up-to-date inputs. Most models separate parameters from state. ARIMA, exponential smoothing, and ML models using lag, rolling mean, and day-of-week features all depend heavily on yesterday and last week, but you get that by feeding yesterday’s sales as a new feature value, not by refitting coefficients. The learned weekly seasonality and trend change slowly, so refitting on a rolling 1.5 years every day adds compute and instability for almost no gain. In practice retrain on a schedule — weekly or monthly — or when performance degrades, promotions or regime shifts occur. Daily refitting makes more sense for online models, simple exponential smoothing with Kalman updating, or highly non-stationary demand where yesterday changes the level. Even then you’d often just update state, not do a full retrain. Validate retrain frequency by backtesting.

question: I'm looking for some common problems in unix system administration and ways that shell scripting can solve them. Completely for self-educational purposes. Also I'd like to know how would you go about learning shell scripting.
answer_raw: Disk full alerts, stale log files, forgotten backups and user accounts that pile up are daily headaches, and tiny shell scripts handle them well. A cron job running df and du with mail can warn before partitions fill, while find with -mtime plus gzip or rm keeps /var/log manageable. Tar over ssh in a nightly script gives you versioned backups without expensive tools, and a loop over a text file with useradd, chpasswd and chown automates onboarding. For monitoring, parsing ps, netstat or journalctl output with grep, awk and wc lets you restart failed services. I learned by automating my own chores first, reading man pages for bash, test, sed and awk, then dissecting scripts in /etc/init.d and on GitHub. Running shellcheck on everything and breaking scripts deliberately taught error handling, set -euo pipefail and logging much faster than any tutorial.

question:
When i installed ubuntu in my x86 machine, I had to configure some memory as 'swap area'.

What is the use of this memory and what is the importance of this memory in linux file systems?

How can I determine the exact size of 'swap area' in a machine for the safe working of linux inside in it?
answer_raw: Swap area acts as virtual RAM extension on disk, giving Linux breathing room when physical memory fills up. Inactive pages are moved there, freeing RAM for active processes and preventing crashes due to out-of-memory errors. It also stores RAM contents during hibernation, allowing a full shutdown without losing session state. While not really part of the filesystem hierarchy, it is managed as a separate partition or file with its own format, invisible to normal file operations. For sizing, old rules suggested double the RAM, but that is excessive today. For machines with less than 2GB RAM, matching RAM size makes sense. With 4 to 8GB, 2 to 4GB of swap is usually enough for desktop use. Servers or systems using hibernation should keep swap equal to or slightly larger than RAM to safely save state.

question: I am changing my current partition scheme (personal development laptop, dual boot) to remove the Windows partition and leave only my Slackware64 instance. What thought should go into my partitioning? I have been keeping / and /home in separate partitions, as well as a swap partition too. How do I decide what other partitions would be good to have in their own section of the disk?
answer_raw: Keep your current approach as a baseline, since isolated /home lets you reinstall Slackware without losing personal files and protects you from a runaway process filling root. Swap is less critical now unless you hibernate or have little RAM; with 16GB+ you can shrink it or use a swapfile instead. Consider splitting out /var because development databases, containers, logs, and package caches can grow unpredictably and fill /. Putting /var or /var/lib/docker on its own partition contains that damage. A separate /boot or EFI system partition is still required for UEFI booting, keep it around 512MB. Separate /tmp as tmpfs in RAM avoids extra partitioning. Don't over-partition; fixed sizes become rigid and one full partition can still break the system while space sits unused elsewhere. Use LVM or leave unallocated space so you can grow later.

question:
How can I find out who executed a particular command and which terminal was used to run it?

Original:

How can I know particular cmd is executed by whom and to know about my terminal
answer_raw: Use the `who` and `w` commands to see logged-in users and their terminals, shown as pts/0, pts/1, tty1, etc. The `whoami` command shows your current username, `id` shows your user and group IDs, and `tty` shows your current terminal device. Use `ps -o user,tty,cmd -p PID` or `ps aux | grep command` to check who owns a running process and which terminal started it. For finished commands, check shell history files like ~/.bash_history, though they rarely record the terminal. For reliable auditing, enable process accounting with `acct` or `auditd`, which logs the user, terminal, time, and full command. On multi-user systems, also check `/var/log/auth.log` or `last` to correlate logins with terminal sessions.

question: Why are tables built into ipchains? What was the benefit of adding tables to ipchains? Is there a simple scenario that would illustrate how tables are used to increase performance or offer some other benefit?
answer_raw:
Tables were added to separate packet processing by function so a packet only hits the rules relevant to its path. In ipchains there was just one linear set of input, forward and output checks, so every packet trudged through masquerading, filtering and mangling logic together even when most didn't apply.

With iptables architecture the kernel defines independent tables like filter, nat, and mangle attached to different Netfilter hooks. A rule lookup stays short and cached for the job at hand, and connection tracking lets established flows bypass expensive lookups.

For example, take a home router doing NAT and firewalling. The first SYN from inside hits the nat table to pick a source port and the filter table to permit it. Reply and follow-on packets match the conntrack entry, so they skip full NAT rule evaluation and just get fast translation plus a quick filter accept for ESTABLISHED. That cuts per-packet work from dozens of rules to two.

question:
I am confused by the dual concepts of time-resolution and bandwidth. Often I will hear that a pulse-compressed radar application 'doesnt have enough BW' for some specific time resolution that is sought.

Isnt the maximum time resolution simply the reciprocal of your sampling rate?

How are those concepts related?
answer_raw: Bandwidth sets how narrow a compressed pulse can be, roughly 1/B in time, which sets range resolution as c/2B. Sampling only sets how finely you record that waveform, with spacing 1/Fs. A system can sample very fast but still produce a wide, blurry matched-filter output if the waveform sweeps little frequency. Two close targets will then merge into one hump no matter how many samples you take, because oversampling merely traces the same blur more smoothly. Conversely you cannot meaningfully use arbitrarily fine physical resolution without sampling fast enough to capture it, with Nyquist requiring Fs at least equal to the bandwidth for complex samples. So saying there is not enough bandwidth means the physics does not support separating echoes that close, even with infinite sampling rate.

question: Can anyone state the difference between frequency response and impulse response in simple English?
answer_raw:
Impulse response is how a system behaves in time after you hit it with a very short, sharp kick. Imagine clapping once in a cathedral and listening to the echo die away. That decaying sound is essentially the impulse response. It tells you about ringing, delays, and reverberation moment by moment.

Frequency response is the same information viewed from the frequency side. Instead of asking what happens over time, it asks how much the system boosts or cuts each pitch, and how much it shifts each pitch in time. Think of turning a bass knob up and treble down on a stereo.

Mathematically they are a Fourier pair: one transforms into the other. If you know one completely, you know the other. Engineers often measure the impulse because it is easy, then convert to frequency response because it is easier to interpret.

question:
I need help understanding how/what does it mean to "turn" a transformation parameters into a vote. I know how to recover the transformation parameters (in my case: 6 DOF), but how this turns into a vote in 6D (??) space ?

Thank You !
answer_raw: Each computed 6 DOF pose is just a point in pose space, with three coordinates for translation and three for rotation, e.g. Euler angles or axis-angle. Voting means you quantize that continuous 6D space into bins and add one count to the bin your estimate falls into. You do this for many noisy estimates derived from different feature correspondences or point triplets. Wrong matches scatter their votes randomly, but correct matches all agree on roughly the same translation and rotation, so they pile up in the same bins and form a peak. You then find the bin with the most votes and optionally refine it by averaging the poses that voted there. In practice you never build a dense 6D array because it would be enormous, so you use a hash table to store only non-empty bins and choose bin sizes to balance tolerance to noise against false peaks.

question:
I performed 512 point FFT on a signal. I got another set of 512 Numbers. I understand that those numbers represent amplitude of the various sine and cosine waves having different frequencies.

If my understanding is correct can somebody tell me how to know the frequencies of those sine and cosine waves from the knowledge of those 512-numbers (i.e amplitudes) ?
answer_raw: Each of the 512 values corresponds to a specific frequency bin determined by your sampling rate. If Fs is the samples per second, bin k centers at k*Fs/512 Hz. Bin 0 is DC, bin 1 is the fundamental at Fs/512, and so on. The frequency resolution is therefore Fs/512, so higher Fs spreads the bins wider. For a real input signal only the first 257 bins are unique, up to the Nyquist frequency Fs/2 at bin 256. Bins 257 to 511 mirror bins 255 down to 1 as complex conjugates and do not represent new positive frequencies. The magnitude you compute from each complex FFT output is proportional to amplitude at that bin frequency, scaled by N/2 for a one-sided spectrum. To find dominant tones, look for peaks in the magnitude of the first half and convert their indices with k*Fs/512.

question:
I have convolved a random signal with a a Gaussian and added noise (Poisson noise in this case) to generate a noisy signal. Now I would like to deconvolve this noisy signal to extract the original signal using the same Gaussian.

The problem is that I need a code which does the job of deconvolution in 1D. (I have already found some in 2D but my main aim is 1D).

Can you please suggest me some packages or programs that are able to do so? (Preferably in MATLAB)

Thanks in advance for the help.
answer_raw: Use deconvlucy in MATLAB with your sampled Gaussian as the PSF, as Lucy-Richardson is specifically derived for Poisson noise and preserves nonnegativity. Although listed as 2D image code it accepts 1D vectors, so you can pass your noisy trace directly and set the iteration count to control sharpness versus noise amplification, using DAMPAR and WEIGHT to stabilize. If convergence is slow or ringing appears, try deconvwnr for Wiener filtering or deconvreg for regularized least-squares, both of which allow you to supply noise-to-signal power ratio and work fine in 1D. For full control implement frequency-domain division yourself by zero-padding the Gaussian to signal length, computing FFTs, then applying H_conj / (|H|^2 + epsilon) weighting before inverse FFT. Always pad edges to reduce circular convolution artifacts and smooth or threshold the result slightly.

question: I know the basic working principle of sinusoidal oscillators. But I have a doubt on this matter when I came across Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization procedure. I have read that the source for sinusoid signal output from an oscillator is the noise. Due to controlled positive feedback a single frequency component is selected and amplified, right? If the noise is a white noise, we say it has all frequency components. We think in terms of all possible sinusoids with different frequencies. When coming to frequency response too, we think in terms of sinusoids. Why can't we think in terms of other orthogonal basis set? Although it makes life difficult, I would like to know the justification for thinking in terms of sinusoids. Is sinusoids the nature's default signals?
answer_raw:
Sinusoids are special for linear time-invariant circuits because they are eigenfunctions. Pass a sinusoid through any LTI filter, amplifier, RC or LC network and you still get a sinusoid of the same frequency, only amplitude and phase change. No other basis has this property; a square wave or Walsh function gets distorted.

White noise can indeed be expanded in any complete orthogonal set, but the oscillator circuit itself does its own filtering by convolution, differentiation and integration. Those operations are diagonalized by complex exponentials, which is why Fourier analysis makes the Barkhausen condition simple: loop gain = 1 at one frequency.

Resonance also favors sinusoids. An LC tank stores energy alternating between L and C, and the solution to its second-order differential equation is naturally sinusoidal. So it is not mysticism, it is mathematics matching physics.

question: What's the correct way. Should I zero-pad a signal before or after applying a windowing function?
answer_raw:
Window first, then zero-pad. Windowing is meant to taper the actual data to reduce spectral leakage from the abrupt edges of the finite segment, so it should only touch the N real samples. If you pad with zeros first and then apply an N+pad-point window, you're distorting the spectrum by tapering zeros and changing the effective window shape, coherent gain and mainlobe width for no benefit.

The usual flow is take your block, multiply by your Hann, Hamming, Blackman, etc. of the same length, then append zeros out to your desired FFT size for interpolation or to hit a power of two. Zero-padding after doesn't add information or improve true resolution, it just interpolates the DTFT bins more finely. One exception is when you intentionally want to do something like whole-frame processing where the window is already designed at the FFT length, but for standard spectral analysis, STFT and measurement, always window the data then pad.

question:
When energy is referred to as the square summable sequence, is that energy a representation of the power of the signal? How is the energy of frequency determined?

E.g. what if an audio signal has high energy on the higher frequencies and another has high energy on the lower, bass, frequencies, how is this determined?

What exactly is the power from the square summable series representing then and is it useful for audio?
answer_raw:
No, finite energy and finite power describe different signal classes. For a discrete signal x[n], the l2 energy is sum |x[n]|^2. If this sum is finite the signal is square summable and has zero average power. Power is instead the time average, the limit of the mean square over a long window, used for persistent sounds that do not decay.

The frequency distribution comes from the Fourier transform. By Parseval’s theorem total energy equals the integral of |X(f)|^2, so |X(f)|^2 acts as energy per frequency. A bass-heavy sound has large |X(f)| at low f, a bright sound at high f, estimated in practice with the DFT or spectrogram over short frames.

For audio the raw infinite sum is rarely used directly, but short-time mean square is highly useful as a measure of loudness, for normalization, compression, and spectral equalization.

question: What's the difference between these? Both are measurements of some form of signal power, but surely there's some difference between the power they are measuring?
answer_raw: dB expresses a relative ratio between two powers, with no fixed reference, so it describes gain, loss, or difference. A 3 dB increase means roughly double the power, and a 10 dB increase means ten times, regardless of the starting level. dBm is absolute because its reference is fixed at 1 milliwatt. 0 dBm equals 1 mW, 30 dBm equals 1 W, and negative values indicate less than 1 mW, as is common in received signals. In practice you use dB for antenna gain, cable loss, or fade margin, and dBm for transmit power, receiver sensitivity, or measured signal strength. You can add or subtract dB to or from dBm to get a new dBm value, but you cannot meaningfully add two dBm figures directly because that would multiply their underlying linear powers.

A 3 dB increase means roughly double the power, and a 10 dB increase means ten times, regardless of the starting level. dBm is absolute because its reference is fixed at 1 milliwatt. 0 dBm equals 1 mW, 30 dBm equals 1 W, and negative values indicate less than 1 mW, as is common in received signals. In practice you use dB for antenna gain, cable loss, or fade margin, and dBm for transmit power, receiver sensitivity, or measured signal strength. question:
My understanding of Pulse Doppler Radar is the system measures Time Of Flight for the pulse.

My confusion is that during the down conversion process prior to ADC the lowpass filter causes some time delay in addition to the time of flight. In principle the delay should be known beforehand but I'm sure it's not exact and in general the delay is not completely constant even among the band of interest.

How is this delay dealt with?
answer_raw:
It is treated as a fixed system bias and calibrated out rather than calculated from first principles. The transmit chain, filters, cables, downconverter, low-pass / anti-alias filter, and ADC all add group delay, but for a given hardware mode and temperature it is largely stable.

Manufacturers measure it with loopback, built-in test, or a target at known range, then subtract that offset in the range equation. Small variations with frequency matter because a filter does not have perfectly flat group delay, which would smear a wideband pulse. That is handled by characterizing the end-to-end impulse response and including it in the matched filter / pulse-compression reference, effectively equalizing the in-band distortion.

Residual drift with temperature, voltage, and component aging is tracked with periodic calibration and stable local oscillators. For Doppler, absolute delay hardly matters anyway since velocity comes from pulse-to-pulse phase change, where common delay cancels.

question:
I want to construct a reference locked sine oscillator. The multibit sine wave is calculated using DDS. The multibit reference signal is typically not sinusoidal, can have offset and substantial noise, but is expected to contain one dominant frequency.

If this dominant frequency is nearly known, a standard PLL approach will work to keep track of the dominant frequency in the reference signal.

However, I now suppose this cannot work to acquire initial reference lock if the dominant frequency is far away from the oscillator frequency. In this case, the PLL gets stuck on a locally dominant frequency.

What is the common approach to resolve this ? Calculating an DFT seems like overkill, since it produces a lot of unnecessary information. A recursive 4 sample Zoom FFT looks a bit more efficient. But maybe there is a way that directly modifies the PLL filter to capture further off frequencies ?

Please let me know if I missed crucial info.
answer_raw: Add a separate coarse frequency acquisition loop in front of the PLL, essentially making it an FLL-assisted PLL. The PLL alone only has a limited pull-in range set by loop bandwidth, so with large initial error it will false-lock to a beat note, harmonic, or noise peak. The standard fix is not to widen the PLL filter – that just admits more noise and risks instability – but to steer the DDS frequency toward zero beat first. In practice this uses a frequency detector rather than a phase detector, or an automatic sweep/search until a lock detector trips, then handoff to narrowband phase tracking. For a nearly-known but possibly far-off tone, zero-crossing period counting, a quadrature-delay discriminator, or autocorrelation is usually enough; a full DFT or zoom FFT is overkill. Missing info is expected frequency uncertainty, SNR and spur levels, allowed acquisition time versus tracking jitter, and whether DC offset is removed, since that sets averaging and sweep rate.
